subject: identification different in bayesian and frequentist?

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: identification different in bayesian and frequentist?
parts:
Hi all

I have an identification question.

I have the following model, it is a piecewise multilevel regression:

Y = B0 + B1*X + B2*(X - D)

as we expand this:

Y = B0 - B2*D + (B1 + B2)*X

In this model only X is known, so we have 1 known and 4 unknow parameters.

I have the model working in stan, and works fine and converged. But, out of bayesian analysis this model would be unidentified since we have a product of 2 unknown parameters (B2*D).

How is that a model like thid is identified in bayesian but is not in the frequentist analysis?

Or maybe i am missing something?

Thanks

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] identification different in bayesian and frequentist?
parts:
It somewhat depends on how you define "identifiable".  

The first difference with a Bayesian analysis will be the presence of priors which, even when weak, will constrain the posterior mass for those 4 parameters into a finite neighborhood (otherwise you wouldn't have had a valid prior in the first place).  Despite this, you can still have non-identifiability in the sense that the posterior will not converge to a point mass in the limit of infinite data.  In a very real sense, however, that doesn't matter because (a) the infinite data limit isn't real anyways and (b) Bayesian inference doesn't report point estimates but rather distributions.  In practice such non-identifiability will result in large correlations between the parameters (perhaps even non-convexity) but a proper Bayesian analysis will identify those correlations.  Even if you report single parameter marginals you'll get distributions that span the marginal variance rather than the conditional variance at any point (which is what a standard frequentist result would quote, and why identifiability is really important there), and it's really the marginal variance that best encodes the uncertainty regarding a parameter.

Simple example:  consider a model with parameters mu1 and mu2 with likelihood N(x | mu1 + mu2, sigma).  No matter how much data you collect, the likelihood will not converge to a point but rather a line mu1 + mu2 = 0.  The conditional variance of mu1 and mu2 at any point on that line will be really small, despite the fact that the parameters can't really be identified.

Bayesian priors constrain the posterior distribution from that line to a long, cigar shaped distribution.  Not easily to sample from but at least compact.  A good Bayesian analysis will explore the entirety of that cigar, either identifying the correlation between mu1 and m2 or returning the marginal variances that correspond to the projection of the long cigar onto the mu1 or mu2 axes, which give a much more faithful summary of the uncertainty in the parameters than the conditional variances.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] identification different in bayesian and frequentist?
parts:
In practice, identifiability in the weak sense is good.

Index swapping in mixture models is trickier. You won't get
a good R-hat there.

For a very deep discussion of this issue, there's
Watanabe's book on "singular" models, of which Michael's
artificial mu1 + mu2 is the poster child for. In this
case, you can monitor mu1+mu2 for convergence and should
be reasonably OK (modulo difficulties in adaptation).

- Bob
